analysis.one_liner: Declares national policy that insurance must cover severe mental illness on par with physical illness.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 24 bipartisan Senate cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would declare it national policy that people with severe mental illnesses — schizophrenia, severe depression, manic-depressive illness — must not be discriminated against in health coverage. Insurance, whether public or private, would have to cover treatment of these illnesses no more restrictively than treatment of major physical illnesses. The bill spells out a model plan: catastrophic stop-loss protection, coverage of facility care and outpatient treatment, psychotherapy visits, and needed prescription drugs, with cost controls built in. It does not itself mandate coverage; instead it commits Congress and the Executive Branch to follow this policy in future health legislation.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of Americans with severe mental illnesses and their families. The bill's findings document how rare fair coverage is: only 21 percent of health insurance policies cover inpatient care for severe mental illness comparably to physical illness, only 2 percent have comparable outpatient coverage, and over 60 percent of HMOs and PPOs specifically exclude such treatment [S3]. A national parity policy would push future health reform legislation to end those restrictions, and the bill notes that treating these illnesses can keep young adults productive and reduce costlier interventions like homelessness, incarceration, and suicide [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Declares that health coverage of severe mental illnesses must be equitable and commensurate with coverage of other major physical illnesses, whether provided publicly or privately [S2][S3].

Defines a model nondiscriminatory plan: stop-loss protection against catastrophic costs, coverage of facility care and outpatient medical management, psychotherapy visits, and essential prescription drugs [S3].
Commits Congress and the Executive Branch to incorporate this parity policy into any future legislation that expands access to or controls the costs of health care [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor plans would bear the cost of extending comparable coverage for mental health treatment, which today only about 2 percent of policies provide adequately [S3]. HMOs and PPOs that currently exclude severe mental illness treatment would have to cover it under the policy standard [S3]. Because the bill is a policy commitment rather than an enforceable mandate, no one pays anything under this bill itself.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself require anyone to cover anything; it is a statement of policy and a model plan, with no enforcement mechanism, so its direct effect would depend entirely on future legislation [S2][S3].

Extending comparable mental health coverage would add costs for insurers and employer-sponsored plans, which is why the model plan builds in cost controls such as precertification review, coinsurance, and managed payment methods [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — ending insurance discrimination against severe mental illness — addresses a documented and severe gap, with real human costs in suicide, homelessness, and incarceration when these treatable illnesses go untreated [S3]. But the bill is deliberately modest in form: it sets a standard and a model rather than mandating coverage, so its immediate effect would be limited to shaping future health reform. The main cost, higher premiums for broader coverage, would fall on insurers and employers, partially offset by the cost-control design and by long-run savings the bill's findings cite [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Pete Domenici introduced the bill with Senator John Danforth on May 12, 1992, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1][S3][S5].
Twenty-four senators — 11 Republicans and 13 Democrats — signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support [S4].
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the bill died at the end of the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, HMOs, and PPOs benefited from the bill's death, because no national policy standard against restrictive mental health coverage was put in place, leaving their existing exclusions and coverage limits intact. Families of people with severe mental illness gained nothing from this Congress, though the parity idea returned in later years. 2456310a1c7b946015a2f3f000fb8cd4df68d6864f6c7b3c4e29a9bebd6cd8dd[0]

for.name: Sen. Pete V. Domenici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 12, 1992, declaring a national policy of equitable insurance coverage for severe mental illnesses.

for.name: Sen. John Danforth
for.what_they_did: Joined Domenici in introducing the bill in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred, chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out; the bill never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: a Republican senator led the bill, and cosponsorship split 11 Republicans to 13 Democrats; no opposition vote is recorded anywhere in the bill's history.

industries.note: The bill's findings document that only 21 percent of policies cover inpatient mental illness care comparably to physical illness and only 2 percent cover outpatient care comparably [S3]. Had its policy become binding law, insurers would have had to extend coverage, bearing the added cost of treatment their plans currently exclude or cap.
Over 60 percent of HMOs and preferred provider organizations specifically exclude treatment for severe mental illnesses, and the bill's policy standard directly targets that practice [S3].
